steps.d: Stiff cardboard or foam board, 2 drinking straws, 2 wooden skewers, 4 bottle caps, a rubber band, a paper clip, tape and glue. It’s all in the kit box.
steps.w: Good engineers start with a plan and a parts list.

steps.d: Take the cardboard rectangle, about 20 by 8 centimeters, and rest it on the little stand so you can work underneath. This is the chassis, the frame everything else attaches to.
steps.w: A stiff, light chassis wastes less energy bending.
steps.act: Set the chassis on the stand

steps.d: Tape the two straws across the bottom, one near each end. Keep them parallel or the car will curve.
steps.w: The straws are bearings: the axles spin inside them with very little friction.

steps.d: Slide a skewer through each straw, leaving a little sticking out on both sides.
steps.w: Axles carry the wheels and let each pair turn together.

steps.d: Poke a hole in the center of each bottle cap and push one onto each axle end. A dab of glue keeps them on.
steps.w: Wheels that are centered and straight roll farther and wobble less.

steps.d: Hook the rubber band on a paper clip taped to the front, and loop the other end around the rear axle.
steps.w: The stretched rubber band stores energy. As it unwinds it spins the rear axle: your engine and drivetrain in one.

steps.d: Fold a body from card stock and set it over the chassis. Keep it light.
steps.w: Less weight lets the same stored energy push the car farther.

steps.d: Roll the car backward to wind the band around the axle, set it down and let go!
steps.w: Real engineers test, measure, change one thing and test again.

steps.d: Craft sticks or wooden skewers, cardboard, glue (a hot glue gun works fast, with an adult’s help), and a tray to use as a shake table. The cards are in the rack and the sticks in the tray.
steps.w: Every structure starts with a plan.

steps.d: Take the cardboard base, with its strip of card glued around the edge, and set it on the shake table.
steps.w: The foundation carries the whole building’s weight down to the ground.

steps.d: Glue a stick upright at each corner.
steps.w: Columns carry weight straight down, like the studs in a wall.

steps.d: Glue sticks across the tops of the columns, then set a piece of card on top as the second floor.
steps.w: Beams tie the columns together and hold up the floor.

steps.d: Repeat: four more columns, four beams and a card roof.
steps.w: Every story adds weight that the floors below have to carry.

steps.d: Glue sticks in an X across the long sides of each story.
steps.w: Triangles can’t change shape, so cross-bracing stops the frame from leaning over, or racking, in an earthquake.

steps.d: Hold the tray and slide it quickly back and forth, like an earthquake.
steps.w: Engineers test real buildings this way on giant shake tables. Compare your frame with and without its bracing.
